chapters.title: Chapter 3: Constructing and Testing a Factor Strategy

lessons.title: Backtesting a Factor Strategy: Look-Ahead Bias, Survivorship Bias, and Data Pitfalls

body.text: A backtest is only as honest as the data it was built on. Most factor strategies that look brilliant on a spreadsheet and fail the moment real money touches them were never actually beaten by the market, they were beaten by a dataset that quietly knew things it should not have known, and quietly forgot the companies that did not survive.

children.text: You now know how to build a factor score. The next question is whether it would actually have worked historically, and that question is far easier to answer wrong than right. This lesson covers the two most damaging, most common backtesting errors, look-ahead bias and survivorship bias, along with the data pitfalls and cost assumptions that separate a backtest that flatters you from one you can trust.
Look-Ahead Bias: Using Information You Wouldn't Have Had Yet

markDefs.definition: A backtesting error where a simulated historical decision uses information that would not actually have been publicly available at that point in time, making the strategy look smarter than it could ever have been in real time.

children.text: creeps in the moment a backtest uses a piece of information before it was actually public. The most common version: tagging a company's quarterly results to the quarter's end date, rather than the date those results were actually filed and disclosed. Under SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, listed companies are required to submit quarterly financial results within 45 days of the quarter's end, and audited annual results within 60 days of the financial year's end. A backtest that rebalances on 31 March using that quarter's results is silently assuming knowledge that, in reality, would not become public for another month and a half.

body.label: SEBI's disclosure timeline
body.context: Under SEBI's LODR Regulations, listed companies must disclose quarterly results within 45 days of quarter-end and audited annual results within 60 days of financial year-end. Any backtest rebalancing on the period-end date itself, rather than the actual disclosure date, is quietly using information from the future.

children.text: Two subtler versions of the same problem show up constantly. First, restated financials: when a company later revises a previously reported number, for example after an audit adjustment, a backtest using today's cleaned-up historical database is often silently using the restated figure rather than what investors actually saw and traded on at the time. Second, backward-filled index membership: building a strategy's universe from 'today's Nifty 200 constituents, applied to the last ten years of data' silently excludes every stock that has since been removed from the index, and includes every stock that has since been added, neither of which reflects the universe an investor actually had to choose from in, say, 2018.
Survivorship Bias: Only Counting the Stocks That Made It

markDefs.definition: A backtesting error where a strategy's historical universe only includes companies that are still listed and trading today, silently excluding companies that were delisted, merged, or went bankrupt along the way.

children.text: Building a ten-year backtest by pulling the price history of every stock currently listed on the NSE is a natural, and dangerously wrong, first instinct. Over any ten-year stretch, some companies get voluntarily or compulsorily delisted, some go through mergers and amalgamations, and some go through insolvency proceedings and effectively cease to exist as investable equity. A backtest built only from today's list of survivors has quietly deleted every one of those failures from history, which is precisely the kind of company a factor screen, especially a naive value or size screen, is statistically more likely to have flagged as attractive in the years before it failed.

body.text: Survivorship bias does not just inflate a backtest's average return, it specifically flatters the exact factor strategies most likely to have owned the failures. A cheap, statistically undervalued stock in a historical database is sometimes cheap because the market correctly saw it heading towards financial distress. If that stock was delisted or went to zero and simply is not in your dataset at all, your backtest never learns this lesson, and neither do you, until it happens with real capital.

children.text: Point-in-Time Data: The Discipline Both Biases Share

Both errors are, at their core, the same mistake wearing different clothes: using a database that reflects what is known today rather than what was known at each historical point in time. The proper fix is a point-in-time, or PIT, database, one that records, for every historical date, exactly which stocks were investable, exactly what financial data had been disclosed by that date, and exactly what each figure said before any later restatement. Building or licensing a genuine point-in-time dataset is unglamorous, expensive, and precisely the kind of infrastructure investment that separates institutional-quality backtesting from a spreadsheet exercise that happens to look impressive.

body.caption: Additional data pitfalls that distort a factor backtest

cells: A stock split, bonus issue, or rights issue changes the share price and share count without changing the business, producing a false 'price crash' or distorted ratio if not adjusted for
Use split- and bonus-adjusted price and share count series throughout
Applying a stock's current sector or industry classification to its historical data can misclassify periods when the company operated a different core business
Use historical, as-of-date sector classifications when sector-neutralising a score
screener.in, exchange filings, and commercial data vendors can define 'adjusted' figures, sector buckets, or even fiscal year-ends slightly differently
Reconcile a sample of figures across sources before trusting a large-scale automated pull

children.text: Even a bias-free backtest is still just a paper exercise until real-world costs are subtracted. In India, that means brokerage, the Securities Transaction Tax charged on equity delivery and derivatives trades, GST on brokerage and other charges, stamp duty, and, most easily underestimated, market impact, the extent to which your own buying or selling moves the price against you, particularly acute for the smaller, less liquid names covered in Chapter 2's size factor lesson. Government-set rates like STT change periodically through the Finance Act, so any specific cost assumption used in a backtest should be checked against current rates rather than assumed to be permanent.

columns.label: Idealised Backtest
points: Trades execute at the exact closing price with zero slippage
Universe includes only stocks that are still listed today
Data is tagged to the period it describes, not the date it was disclosed
No brokerage, STT, GST, or stamp duty deducted from returns

columns.label: Realistic Implementation
points: Trades incur bid-ask spread and market impact, larger for smaller, less liquid names
Universe is point-in-time correct, including stocks later delisted, merged, or gone bankrupt
Every data point is timestamped to its actual public disclosure date
Brokerage, STT, GST, stamp duty, and rebalancing turnover are all deducted from returns

body.title: Backtest Pre-Flight Checklist
steps: Confirm the universe includes stocks that were later delisted, merged, or went through insolvency, not just today's survivors
Confirm every financial data point is timestamped to its actual public disclosure date, respecting SEBI's 45-day (quarterly) and 60-day (annual) disclosure windows, not the period-end date
Confirm index or sector membership is historical, as-of-date, not backward-filled from today's list
Confirm prices and share counts are adjusted for splits, bonus issues, and rights issues throughout
Confirm realistic transaction costs, brokerage, STT, GST, stamp duty, and market impact, are deducted, especially for less liquid names
Reconcile a sample of figures across at least two independent data sources before trusting a full-scale automated pull

body.title: Spot the Bias
body.scenario: A junior analyst presents a ten-year backtest of a value strategy on NSE-listed stocks. They explain their process: 'I pulled the current constituent list of the Nifty 500, downloaded ten years of price and fundamental data for each of those companies, and rebalanced the portfolio every 31 March using that fiscal year's annual results.'
body.prompt: Identify at least two distinct biases in this process, and explain what each one would likely do to the backtest's reported returns.
body.modelAnswer: First, this is survivorship bias: using the current Nifty 500 constituent list to pull ten years of history silently excludes any company that was delisted, merged, or went bankrupt during that period, which would likely inflate the backtest's reported returns since some of the worst-performing, most statistically 'cheap' stocks in history are exactly the ones that failed and dropped out of today's list. Second, this is look-ahead bias: rebalancing on 31 March using that fiscal year's annual results assumes those audited results were available on the same day the fiscal year ended, when SEBI's LODR regulations actually give companies up to 60 days after year-end to disclose audited annual results, meaning the backtest is using information roughly two months before it would have actually been public. Both errors push the backtest's reported performance to look better than a real, live strategy could have achieved.

body.title: Test Yourself: Point-in-Time Data
body.question: What is the defining feature of a genuine point-in-time (PIT) database, as opposed to a standard 'as reported today' database?
options: It only contains data from the most recent five years
It records exactly what data was known and which stocks were investable as of each historical date, including later-restated figures and later-delisted stocks
It automatically adjusts all historical prices to today's currency value
It only includes large-cap stocks to simplify the dataset
body.explanation: A point-in-time database preserves history exactly as it looked on each historical date, including original (not restated) figures and stocks that were later delisted or merged, which is precisely what is needed to avoid both look-ahead and survivorship bias.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: Using information in a backtest before it would actually have been publicly available at that point in time, such as tagging results to a period-end date rather than the actual disclosure date.
Building a backtest's universe only from companies still listed today, silently excluding companies that were delisted, merged, or went bankrupt during the historical period being tested.
A dataset that preserves exactly what was known, and which stocks were investable, as of each historical date, rather than reflecting today's restated figures and surviving universe.
The extent to which a trader's own buying or selling activity moves the price against them, a cost that is often ignored in idealised backtests but can be substantial for less liquid stocks.

body.text: This lesson describes general backtesting principles for educational purposes and is not a complete guide to building production-grade backtesting infrastructure. Specific SEBI disclosure timelines and tax rates such as STT are subject to change; always verify current regulations directly with SEBI and the applicable Finance Act before relying on them.

points: Look-ahead bias uses information before it would actually have been public, most commonly by tagging financial results to the period-end date instead of the actual disclosure date, which SEBI's LODR regulations set at 45 days (quarterly) and 60 days (annual)

Survivorship bias builds a backtest universe only from stocks still listed today, silently deleting delisted, merged, or bankrupt companies, exactly the kind of company a naive factor screen may have flagged as attractive before it failed
A genuine point-in-time database, preserving exactly what was known and investable as of each historical date, is the shared fix for both biases
Unadjusted corporate actions, backward-filled sector classifications, and inconsistent data vendor definitions are further pitfalls that can quietly distort a backtest
Realistic implementation requires deducting brokerage, STT, GST, stamp duty, and market impact, none of which appear in an idealised, closing-price-only backtest

A short pre-flight checklist, universe survivorship, disclosure timing, corporate action adjustment, and realistic costs, catches most of the errors that make a backtest look better than a real strategy ever could
